rationale: Tests identification of the Big Four species by their key distinguishing features
Targets the tourniquet misconception — the single most common dangerous first-aid error
Confirms understanding of the two distinct envenomation syndromes and their pathophysiological basis
Tests correct technique and interpretation of the 20WBCT — the cornerstone bedside test for haematotoxic envenomation
Tests the critical distinction that local swelling alone is NOT an antivenom indication
Tests the key pharmacological fact that Indian polyvalent ASV covers both haematotoxic and neurotoxic big-four species
Tests management of antivenom adverse reaction — specifically the role of IM adrenaline (not IV antihistamine first)
Reinforces neostigmine/atropine utility for neurotoxic (elapid) envenomation as adjunct to ASV
Tests the critical prazosin vs beta-blocker distinction — the most dangerous management error in scorpion envenomation
Confirms understanding of the bidirectional autonomic storm and why initial hypertension can be followed by hypotension
Tests the critical route and drug choice for anaphylaxis from bee sting — IM adrenaline, not IV, and not antihistamine first
Confirms the key principle that mass envenomation (hundreds of stings) causes toxicity by a different mechanism than anaphylaxis
